Strategy, Architecture, and Governance
1. Governance, risk and exceptions
Governance, risk, internal control and exceptions

Technology-enabled projects must operate under approved NDIA governance that assigns accountable owners, manages delivery, security, shared and emerging risks against NDIA risk appetite, maintains internal controls, and records any approved exceptions, compensating controls, expiry dates and escalation decisions.

Each technology-enabled project must have approved governance before work starts. It must name accountable owners, manage delivery, security and shared risks, keep key controls, and record any exception with an owner, controls and end date.

Critical

2. Investment, assurance and benefits
Portfolio investment, assurance, gate decisions and benefits

Project proposals and gate decisions must align with NDIA corporate, digital investment and portfolio priorities; document options, costs, benefits, dependencies and risks; complete required IOF, DTA, contestability and assurance reviews; and track benefits, conditions and assurance actions through implementation and post-implementation review.

Project proposals and gate decisions must show that the project supports NDIA strategy and digital investment priorities. They must record options, costs, benefits, dependencies, risks, assurance actions and benefit tracking through delivery and review.

3. Architecture, reuse and interoperability
Architecture review, reuse, interoperability and integration

Projects must complete architecture review before procurement or build, reuse existing NDIA, Commonwealth or market capabilities where practical, and design new solutions with reusable components, APIs, interoperability, integration standards, supportability and clear operational ownership.

Before buying or building technology, the project must complete architecture review. It must reuse existing NDIA, Commonwealth or market capabilities where practical, and design any new component so it can integrate, be supported and be reused.

4. Participants, privacy and protected information
Participant-centred legal authority, privacy and protected Agency information

Projects must confirm legal authority and business ownership, assess participant, provider and staff impacts, maintain traceable Scheme business rules and review pathways, and apply privacy-by-design and protected Agency information controls to all personal or NDIS information handling, including supplier handling.

Projects must confirm they have legal authority and a business owner for any use of participant, provider or staff information. Privacy must be built in from the start, including clear business rules, review pathways and controls for NDIA and supplier handling of protected information.

5. Classification, access and data sharing

Projects must classify information and data holdings, apply required markings, caveats and handling controls, restrict access and external, offshore or international sharing to authorised need-to-know arrangements, and use DATA Scheme data sharing agreements and safeguards only where approved.

Projects must classify information and data, mark it correctly, and limit access or sharing to people and organisations with an authorised need to know. 6. Records, FOI, retention and disposal
Records, FOI readiness, metadata, retention, disposal and decommissioning

Projects must create, store and maintain complete auditable records, metadata, FOI-searchable evidence and decision trails in approved systems, and retain, transfer, decommission or dispose of information and technology assets only under approved records, security and disposal authorities.

Projects must create and keep accurate records of decisions, approvals, designs, testing and operations in approved NDIA systems. Records must be searchable for FOI and audit, and data or technology assets must only be retained, transferred, decommissioned or disposed of under approved authorities.

7. Secure technology lifecycle and authorisation
Secure-by-design lifecycle, system definition, change control and authorisation

Projects must apply an ISM-aligned secure technology lifecycle by defining system boundaries, security objectives, classifications, owners, authorised technology registers and material change triggers; prohibited or legacy technology must have approved mitigations, and no system may go live or continue after material change until residual risk is assessed and authorised.

Projects must use a secure-by-design lifecycle. They must define the system boundary, owners, security goals, classification and change triggers, record the technology in approved registers, and get residual risk authorised before go-live or after a material change.
Mandatory policy requirement
Critical

Cloud, hosting, outsourced ICT, gateways and shared responsibility

Projects that use cloud, hosting, gateways, data centres or outsourced ICT must check security and hosting evidence before approval. They must define who is responsible for each control, where data is stored, how services are monitored, backed up, recovered, costed and exited.
